transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-01-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Anya Lebedev (Redwood SE), Evelyn Ross (Zephyra), Marco Diaz (Zephyra), Sofia Nguyen (Zephyra), Jon Park (Zephyra), Lena Moroz (Zephyra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Intro + partner fit: Zephyra is an HPC-focused cloud provider targeting telecom and financial sims, wants Redwood to run as a private/on-prem conduit for customer inference workloads.
- Discussed networking models, VPC peering, and binary compatibility for custom GPU drivers; need to validate AMIs/OVAs and container runtimes.
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS/HSM, audit logs required.
- Next: sample workload, SOC2 docs, compatibility heatmap, pilot proposal.

Topics: Partner intro; GPU image compatibility; VPC/on-prem deployment patterns; Dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs; Security/compliance; Pilot scoping and success metrics

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros from Redwood side, this is Maya, AE, with Ravi and Anya on the technical side, i'll hand it over to you ravi to kick off the tech context in a sec.
[00:12] Evelyn Ross: hi all, Evelyn here, thanks for doing this, excited to see how Redwood might fit into our conduit product, we run a lot of heavy models for gen-sim and real-time inference for telco customers.
[00:22] Marco Diaz: marco, infra lead. We operate a mix of cloud-native regions and on-prem racks that have a custom kernel and driver stack for a100-v5-derived cards, and we want to understand compatibility and route integration.
[00:35] Ravi Patel: sweet, thanks. quick agenda: partner goals, deployment options, perf/compat risk areas, security, and pilot ask. We'll try to keep it concrete.
[00:44] Jon Park: quick Q up front — we already maintain a lightweight orchestrator called ZephCon, do you have experience integrating with third-party schedulers or do we have to run your agent?
[00:55] Anya Lebedev: great question — we support multiple integration options: direct OCI/RPM images, a light footprint agent for telemetry, or kube-adapter if you want us to plug into k8s. there are tradeoffs depending on your network isolation constraints.
[01:12] Lena Moroz: is there a hard requirement to use Redwood Dedicated or can this run fully within our VPC/private control plane?
[01:20] Maya Chen: you can pick — Redwood Private supports a private control plane with customer-managed networking and on-prem packaging, so you can keep the control plane on your side. Dedicated is more about reserved capacity in our hosting; they are different product modes.
[01:36] Marco Diaz: okay that's helpful, network-wise we prefer VPC peering with strict egress rules and we use JUNOS appliances in edge POPs. would peering be enough?
[01:48] Ravi Patel: peering can work, yes — we typically use VPC peering or direct connect style links. For strict egress we can do an outbound-only policy and mTLS between components. but i want to call out a risk area: your custom driver/kernel — sometimes inference kernels are sensitive to driver mismatches, so we should validate at the binary/kernel level.
[02:08] Marco Diaz: yes that's the crux. our images use a patched cuda runtime and a custom low-level driver for our telemetry overlays. How do you validate that?
[02:19] Anya Lebedev: we have a compatibility harness: you can provide AMIs/OVAs or container runtimes, we run microbenchmarks (mem throughput, attention kernel checks, kv-cache sanity) and a small model trace to see if there's silent degradation. We'll produce a heatmap and remediation notes.
[02:37] Marco Diaz: the term "kv-cache" came through as "K V cache" in some docs last time, haha — ok understood.
[02:45] Sofia Nguyen: from security POV, we require SOC2 Type 2, SSO via SAML/Okta, RBAC, and KMS integration (we use Vault with HSM-backed keys). We need to know if Redwood's private plane can integrate with our KMS and if logs meet our retention policies.
[03:02] Ravi Patel: absolutely — Redwood Private supports KMS integrations and HSM if it's customer-managed. For logs, our console can export audit trails; retention windows are configurable. we'll share our security pack with SOC2 attestation and the KMS integration notes.
[03:18] Evelyn Ross: are there any compliance red flags for financial workloads? we sometimes process trade sims that require audit-ready logs and data residency.
[03:27] Maya Chen: no red flags, it's mostly an ops and agreement conversation. we do have customers in finance running Dedicated and Private; the keys are region pinning and strict audit logging. we'll also include options for encrypted-at-rest models and tokenization if needed.
[03:45] Marco Diaz: ok can you talk about latency and batching controls? a lot of our customers need sub-50ms p99 for small prompts.
[03:53] Anya Lebedev: yeah, sub-50ms p99 with the right model and hardware is feasible but depends on batching. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching and per-route latency SLOs. we can pin a model variant, run small-batch inference, and use prefix caching to keep latency low. there will be a tradeoff with cost though.
[04:14] Jon Park: do you do quantization? we sometimes run q4 variants to reduce memory footprint.
[04:18] Ravi Patel: yes, we have quantization profiles and quantized kernels; the runtime will pick kernels accordingly. the bigger caveat is quality regression — we pair quant recommendations with evals on your prompt set.
[04:33] Lena Moroz: pilot sizing? what would a quick pilot look like if we want to validate both perf and integration?
[04:39] Maya Chen: typical pilot is 4–6 weeks: week 1 onboarding and image validation, week 2 perf benchmark and small traffic test, weeks 3–4 canary traffic and operational runbook testing, plus a final report. We can scope a dedicated pool or run it in your VPC.
[04:58] Marco Diaz: price signals — are there burst/billing concerns if we hit high throughput in pilot?
[05:04] Maya Chen: we'll propose a pilot commercial sketch with an agreed capacity limit; for Dedicated we do reserved capacity sketches and for Private we charge a platform fee plus support. we'll add burst protection policies.
[05:16] Sofia Nguyen: curious about agent/collector telemetry surface area. we cannot allow egress of PII and need field-level filtering on traces.
[05:27] Anya Lebedev: our agent supports scrub rules and you can run it in a restricted mode where no payload leaves the VPC; only metadata summaries for ops telemetry are sent to the control plane if you opt-in. There's also an offline log aggregation mode for air-gapped installs.
[05:45] Marco Diaz: great. what's the longest outage/recovery story for any major upgrade? we need to understand upgrade windows for kernel/driver updates.
[05:54] Ravi Patel: for on-prem we recommend a canary/rolling upgrade path — the runtime supports automatic fallback to a pinned model variant if an upgrade increases latency or errors. we've had upgrades where a small percentage of nodes needed reimage, recovery in hours not days, but it depends on your patch policies.
[06:15] Jon Park: you mentioned fallback — does that require a second model variant on standby consuming resources?
[06:21] Anya Lebedev: it can be an identical model in a different Q-config or a smaller variant; we support warm standby to reduce cold-start. tradeoff is cost vs reliability.
[06:33] Evelyn Ross: who normally owns maintaining the kernel/driver layer in these integrations? our preference is to keep driver maintenance with Zephyra but let Redwood integrate to the exposed runtime.
[06:43] Maya Chen: that's typical — customer maintains kernel/driver, Redwood focuses on runtime and container layers. though for deeply integrated partners we do co-maintenance agreements.
[06:53] Marco Diaz: ok can you outline the artefacts we'll get post-compat test?
[06:58] Ravi Patel: compatibility heatmap, microbenchmark logs, kv-cache sanity checks, example remediation steps if a driver mismatch is detected, and a recommended pilot config (instances, batch sizes, SLO targets).
[07:12] Sofia Nguyen: what's your control plane topology for Private mode? is it a single tenant control plane or multi-tenant with isolation?
[07:20] Anya Lebedev: for Redwood Private it's a private control plane deployed into your environment — single-tenant logical control plane. We can also do an on-prem package for fully air-gapped installs.
[07:31] Marco Diaz: talking about network — do you need inbound firewall rules to our compute nodes? we prefer agents that originate outbound to avoid inbound holes.
[07:40] Ravi Patel: outbound-only agents are fine — most installs use outbound mTLS to the control plane or a message queue in your VPC. inbound is optional for advanced debugging.
[07:51] Lena Moroz: curious about any known issues with our GPU type (we use an a100-v5 family with custom power capping).
[07:59] Ravi Patel: power capping can affect peak throughput; we'll surface that in the heatmap. also some attention kernel implementations assume certain clock rates, so we'll check tail-latency regressions.
[08:12] Evelyn Ross: any references in telco space?
[08:15] Maya Chen: yes we have a couple of telco customers in EMEA, we'll share sanitized case studies.
[08:22] Marco Diaz: ok timelines — we want a pilot to start late Jan if possible. Is that realistic?
[08:27] Maya Chen: yes, assuming we get the AMI/container images and security docs this week or early next week we can align resources for a Jan 22 start.
[08:36] Jon Park: what success metrics do you propose for the pilot?
[08:40] Maya Chen: measurable success criteria: p99 latency below agreed threshold (you suggested 50ms), error rate less than 0.1% under pilot load, and a conclusive compatibility score (no silent kernel regressions). also operational readiness: SSO and audit logs validated.
[08:55] Marco Diaz: who's the single point of contact on Redwood for the pilot?
[08:58] Maya Chen: that'll be me for the program and Ravi for technical execution; Anya will run the compatibility harness.
[09:06] Sofia Nguyen: we need contractual language about data residency and a commitment to not ingest payloads into Redwood-hosted analytics during the pilot.
[09:14] Maya Chen: understood, we'll draft controlled language; Redwood's private mode and dedicated options are designed for that.
[09:22] Marco Diaz: any blockers you foresee?
[09:25] Ravi Patel: the main blocker is if a driver-level incompatibility requires vendor kernel changes — that can add weeks to remediation. we'll know after the compatibility run.
[09:34] Evelyn Ross: ok, logistics — we want your security pack, and we'll send a topology diagram and the sample inference trace by Friday.
[09:41] Maya Chen: perfect. we'll send the integration checklist and SOC2 pack today.
[09:45] (crosstalk)
[09:49] Anya Lebedev: one more note — when you share sample workloads, include both short prompt sets and longer dialogue traces; different caching behaviors surface different issues.
[09:58] Marco Diaz: will do.
[10:01] Maya Chen: recap — action items and owners as we discussed, pilot target week of Jan 22, send artifacts. anything else?
[10:08] Lena Moroz: no, thanks.
[10:10] Evelyn Ross: thanks everyone.
[10:12] Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up with notes and calendar invites.

End of meeting.

We had a productive intro focused on compatibility for Zephyra's custom GPU/driver environment and the networking/security model for a Private deployment. Redwood committed to run a compatibility heatmap against Zephyra images/containers, share SOC2/KMS integration docs, and propose a 4–6 week pilot starting week of 2029-01-22 assuming artifacts are delivered. Primary risks: driver-level mismatches and potential need for kernel/vendor patches. Next meeting: pilot planning session week of 2029-01-15 (tentative).
